Social justice issues are on an upward trend right now, with all the crazy euphemisms and new definitions for "racism" and "sexism" and other nutty stuff that should have stayed on the college campuses. A lot of traditional media outlets are giving the issue the polite treatment - if people want to rant and froth about social justice on camera that is fine, the viewers think it is entertaining. But there is already a growing backlash against the trend, which was pretty predictable given the crazy stories that are being told, like for example the UVA/Rolling Stone rape story which was, in case you didn't hear, completely phony.

So along comes reddit and they are looking to ride this trend upwards for a while, and they have two ways they can do this: they can promote and support the narrative they think people want to hear, and they can quash and censor stuff that goes against the narrative. The problem with the latter approach is that once you bring out the big guns (a.k.a. ban hammers) you have to hold or advance from that position. Thus all of the comments about "Why FPH and not this other group? Aren't you committed to the cause?" And of course no one will ever really know how many more subreddits and accounts were banned since this started on Wednesday, but they clearly decided to hold the line.

Now reddit is in a trap. They must show a continued commitment to the "safe spaces" policy and continue to shut down offending areas, but they have to do it at a speed that doesn't drive away traffic faster than it can be replaced. Plus there is the chilling effect that is already taking hold, actual participation in the site is going to decrease because censorship is no longer an abstract threat. It doesn't really matter if the site gets overrun by the SJW crowd or not, if the majority of the users stop participating then there won't be anything to get angry about.
